This judgmentcumaward shall decide the claim of petitioner Mohd. Mursid  filed under Sections 166 and 140 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (hereinafter  referred to as "M.V. Act") as amended up to date to claim compensation for the  injuries sustained by him in a road vehicular accident that took place on  14.11.2013.

FIR No.435/13 u/ss 279/337 IPC was registered at Police Station  Janak Puri and chargesheet was filed against respondent No.1/Rajesh Ohri,
 drivercumowner of Car bearing registration No.DL7CN1867 (offending  vehicle).
 2 2.
Detailed Accident Report (DAR) was filed by the Investigating Officer (IO) along  with copies of the criminal proceedings including FIR and chargesheet.

sentences.text: Brief facts of the vehicular accident as averred in the claim petition as well as  DAR are that at about 07:00 PM on 14.11.2013, petitioner/injured Mohd.Mursid  was going on his scooty bearing registration No.PB10DV9185.

When he  reached near B1, Super Bazar road, Janak Puri, the offending vehicle came at a  high speed in a rash and negligent manner and after overtaking scooty of the  petitioner, took a sharp right turn.
During the said process, the scooty of the  petitioner and offending vehicle collided with each other.
Resultantly, petitioner  sustained grievous injuries.
Thereafter, he was removed to DDU Hospital for  treatment.

4. Subsequently, it transpired that the offending vehicle was owned and driven by  respondent No.1/Rajesh Ohri and insured with respondent No.2/United India  Insurance Company Ltd.
5.

In the Written Statement filed on behalf of respondent No.1, it was averred that  the accident was caused due to sole negligence of petitioner as he was a minor  and driving two wheeler without any driving licence.

It was further averred that  it is evident from the site plan as well as Mechanical Inspection Report of the car  that alleged offending vehicle was struck on the left side, meaning thereby, that  injured/petitioner had struck his scooty against the car while the car had come  forward to cross the road.

It was stated that since the alleged offending vehicle  was duly insured with respondent No.2/insurance company, hence, no liability  could be fastened upon respondent No.1.
6.

In the Written Statement filed on behalf of respondent No.2/insurance company,
 it was admitted that the alleged offending vehicle was insured with respondent  No.2 vide its Policy bearing No.0406033112P014972 valid from 31.12.2020 to  30.12.2013.
7.

From the pleadings of the parties, contentions raised and material on record, the  following issues were framed by the Learned Predecessor of this Tribunal vide  order dated 09.03.2015:
 ISSUES:
 1.

Whether the petitioner suffered injuries in an accident that took place  on 14.11.2013 at about 7 PM involving car bearing No.DL7CN1867  3  driven/owned by respondent No.1 and insured with respondent No.2?
 OPP  2.
Whether the petitioner is entitled for compensation?

If so, to what  amount and from whom?
 3. Relief 8.
I have heard learned counsels for the parties and have carefully perused the  court record.

9. My findings on the issues are as under:
 Issue No.1:

Whether the petitioner suffered injuries in an accident that took place  on 14.11.2013 at about 7 PM involving car bearing No.DL7CN1867  driven/owned by respondent No.1 and insured with respondent No.2?
 OPP 10.

In a claim petition filed under u/s 166/140 of the M.V. Act, onus is on the  claimant(s)/petitioner(s) to prove that he or she sustained injuries in a vehicular Mohd. Mursid @ Bablu vs Rajesh Ohri on 25 February, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/44431814/
2  accident caused by the wrongful act or negligence of the driver of the offending  vehicle.

11. In support of his claim, petitioner examined Dr.Perminder Kaur, CMO(SAG),
 GGSG Hospital as PW1; ASI Narender Kumar, IO as PW2; Ghyanshyam Lal,
 Senior Executive Medical Record, Kalra Hospital as PW3; Amit Sharma, MRD  Incharge, Orchid Hospital as PW4; Sachin Kumar, Partner of Ananya  International as PW5 (inadvertently mentioned as PW4).
12. Admittedly, neither the petitioner stepped in the witness box nor the petitioner  examined any eyewitness to the accident in question.
It was thus, very  vehemently argued by learned counsel for the insurance company that the  petitioner had failed to prove negligence of the offending vehicle.
It was also  urged that in such circumstances, the outcome of issue No.1 would hinge upon  the testimony of respondent No.1/drivercumowner of the offending vehicle.

13. Per contra, it was contended by learned counsel for petitioner that even though  petitioner did not step in the witness box, the negligence of respondent No.1 in  causing the accident was proved by testimony of PW2/ASI Narendra Kumar,
 who had recorded the statement of petitioner on 30.10.2014 and had proved the  4  same as Ex.PW2/R1/1, wherein, the petitioner had imputed negligence of the  offending vehicle in the accident in question.
14. The argument of learned counsel for petitioner does not hold any water as it is  difficult to believe that any statement (Ex.PW2/R1/1) was given by the  petitioner to PW2/ASI Narendra Kumar.
The medical treatment record of  petitioner Mohd. Murshid reflects that he had sustained severe head injury with  polytrauma, fracture right wrist joint.
He was admitted to Kalra Hospital on  15.11.2013 and discharged on 28.11.2013 against Medical Advise.
At the time  of being declared LAMA, the petitioner was on ventilatory support and his  condition was critical.
It is pertinent to mention here that the petitioner has  sustained 100% permanent disability.

As per disability certificate (Ex.PW1/A),
 petitioner was a case of RTA with head injury with MRI reported as Chronic  wallerian degeneration (with haemorrhages in part of brainstem along with  astrophic changes) with Quadriparesis (dense/severe weakness of all four limbs)
 with severe Bladder involvement (incontinence of urine and stool) along with no  speed output and Neuropsychological impairment.
If the condition of the  petitioner was so severe, it is not possible that petitioner would have given  statement (Ex.PW2/R1/1).
Also, no document was placed on record on behalf of  the petitioner to show that on 30.11.2014, the petitioner was in a condition to  speak and to understand.
Moreover, Ex.PW2/R1/1 does not bear any signatures  of the petitioner.

Rather, a right thumb impression was affixed on the statement  which creates a suspicion regarding the author of Ex.PW2/R1/1.
15.
Be that as it may, factum of accident was not denied by respondent No.1/driver  cumowner of offending vehicle.

So far as negligence is concerned, it was  testified by respondent No.1/Rajesh Ohri/R1W1 in his evidence by way of  affidavit (Ex.R1W1/A) that the scooty being driven by petitioner had struck  against the left side of vehicle of respondent No.1 when respondent No.1 was  taking a Uturn, proceeding towards the road in between Block B1 B3, Super  Bazar Road.

According to the road safety rules, the vehicle proceeding on the  main road has the first right of way and any vehicle is trying to negotiate a U  turn in a road perpendicular to the main road, has to give way to the vehicle  which is proceeding on the main road.

Considering the admission of  5 Mohd. Mursid @ Bablu vs Rajesh Ohri on 25 February, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/44431814/
3  R1W1/respondent No.1 that the petitioner was coming on the main road and  had struck against his vehicle on the left side when respondent No.1 was taking  a Uturn, it is evident that it was respondent No.1 who was negligent and had  ignored the scooty of the petitioner proceeding on the main road.

sentences.text: The said fact  is also corroborated by the site plan and Mechanical Inspection Reports of both  the vehicles which reflect that the offending vehicle was damaged from the left  lower side whereas, the scooty being driven by the petitioner was damaged from  the front lower portion.
16. In view of the given circumstances, it is evident that the accident had taken  place due to negligence of respondent No.1/Rajesh Ohri.
Accordingly, issue  No.1 is decided in favour of the petitioner and against the respondents.

17. Finding on Issue No.2:
 Whether the petitioner is entitled for compensation?

If so, to what  amount and from whom?
18.
In RAJ KUMAR VS. AJAY KUMAR & ANOTHER (2011) 1 SCC 343, Hon'ble  Supreme Court of India has laid down general principles for computation of  compensation in injury cases.

sentences.text:
The relevant paras of the judgment are reproduced  as under:
 5.

The provision of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 ("the Act", for short) makes   clear that the award must be just, which means that compensation should, to  the extent possible, fully and adequately restore the claimant to the position  prior to the accident.

The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss  suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair,
 reasonable and equitable manner.

The court or the Tribunal shall have to  assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation  or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability an  its consequences, is inevitable
. A person is not only to be compensated for th  physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such  injury.

This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a fu  life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoye  but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or  could have earned.

6. The heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases  are the following:
 Pecuniary damages (special damages)
 (i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization, medicines, transportation,
 nourishing food and miscellaneous expenditure.

6  Nonpecuniary damages (general damages)
 (iv) Damages to pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries.

(v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage)
 (vi) Loss of expectation of life (shortening of normal longevity).
In routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under  heads (i), (ii), (a) and (iv).

It is only in serious cases of injury, where the  specific medical evidence corroborating the evidence of the claimant, that  compensation will be granted under any of the heads (ii), (b), (iii), (v) and Mohd. 4  (vi) relating to loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability,
 future medical expenses, loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of  marriage) and loss of expectation of life.

sentences.text:
PECUNIARY DAMAGES (Special Damages)
 Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization and medicines 19.
Petitioner placed on record his medical treatment record and bills.
The bare  perusal of the treatment record reflects that petitioner was suffering from severe  head injury and fracture.

20. During proceedings, it was admitted by the learned c  injured/petitioner that all the expenses related to treatment and hospitalization  of the petitioner were borne by the employer of the petitioner.
In the said  circumstances, it is held that petitioner is not entitled to any compensation  under this head.
Loss of future earning on account of permanent disability 21.
To prove that petitioner sustained 100% physical disability, he examined  PW1/Dr.Perminder Kaur.
PW1/Dr.Perminder Kaur testified that on the basis of  report received from G.B. Pant Hospital, disability certificate (Ex.PW1/A) was  issued in respect of petitioner Mohd.Murshid.
As per Ex.PW1/A, petitioner  Mohd. Murshid sustained 100% permanent disability which was unlikely to  improve.

22. In his crossexamination, PW1/Dr.Perminder Kaur testified that patient  Mohd.Murshid was first examined at Guru Gobind Singh Govt.Hospital and  thereafter, he was referred to G.B. Pant Hospital and on the basis of report of  G.B. Pant Hospital, disability certificate (Ex.PW1/A) was issued.
She  categorically testified that 100% disability sustained by the petitioner was  related to his whole body.

The bare perusal of disability certificate (Ex.PW1/A)
 reflects that petitioner was a case of RTA with head injury with MRI reported as  Chronic wallerian degeneration (with haemorrhages in part of brainstem along  7  with astrophic changes) with Quadriparesis (dense/severe weakness of all four  limbs) with severe Bladder involvement (incontinence of urine and stool) along  with no speed output and Neuropsychological impairment.
23.

In view of testimony of PW1 coupled with the treatment record of the petitioner,
 the functional disability of the petitioner is assessed as 100%.
Compensation on account of loss of earning capacity 24.
It was claimed by the petitioner that at the time of accident, he was doing a  private job and earning Rs.15,000/ per month.

To substantiate his claim,
 petitioner examined PW4/Sachin Kumar, Partner of Ananya International.
In his  testimony, PW4/Sachin Kumar stated that petitioner Mohd.Murshid @ Bablu  was his employee and was working with him as Office Assistant.

He further  stated that petitioner had joined his firm in the year 2010 as Peon/Class IV  employee at a salary of Rs.8,000/ per month but subsequently, in the year  2013, he was promoted to the post of Office Assistant at a monthly salary of  Rs.15,000/.

He placed on record salary certificate issued in respect of petitioner  as Ex.PW4/A.
25.
In his crossexamination by insurance company, PW4/Sachin Kumar testified  that in the year 2013, he had only two employees i.e. petitioner and the name of  other employee he did not remember.
He further testified that he used to give  salary to his employees in cash against voucher.

26. So far as, the monthly income of petitioner is concerned, the testimony of  PW4/Sachin Kumar does not inspire confidence as he failed to produce any Mohd. Mursid @ Bablu vs Rajesh Ohri on 25 February, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/44431814/
5  document for disbursement of salary to the petitioner.

MOHAN AND OTHERS, reported as 2018 ACJ  1011 delivered by three Judges Bench of Hon'ble Supreme Court, the Hon'ble  Supreme Court awarded compensation towards loss of future prospects in a case  where the petitioner had sustained physical disability of 90% due to amputation  of both his hands.

Thus, total monthly income of the  petitioner after making an addition of future prospects would be Rs.11,320.40  per month.
30. Accordingly, loss of future earning on account of physical disability of petitioner  amounts to Rs.11,320.40 per month (Rs.11,320.40 x 100/100).
Hence, annual  loss of future earning of the petitioner is assessed as Rs.1,35,844.80  (Rs.11,320.40 x 12) which is ascertained as multiplicand.

Since petitioner was aged 20 years at the time of the accident, hence, applying  the criteria of multiplier laid down in SARLA VERMA AND OTHERS VS. DELHI  TRANSPORT CORPORATION AND ANOTHER, (2009) 6 SUPREME COURT CASES  121, the multiplier applicable in this case would be 18 (eighteen).

34. Petitioner is further awarded a compensation of Rs.2,00,000/ (Rupees Two  Lakhs) towards attendant charges as it is evident from the testimonies of  PW1/Dr.Parminder Kaur that the petitioner is as good as immobile and is  dependent on others, even for his basic necessities.

9 NONPECUNIARY DAMAGES (GENERAL DAMAGES)
 Pain, Suffering & Trauma 35.

In R.D. HATTANGADI VS. PEST CONTROL (INDIA) PVT.LTD., I (1995) ACC 281  (SC), where a road accident resulted in 100% disability due to paraplegia below  waist to a lawyer (retired Judge), the Supreme Court observed as under:
 "That no amount of compensation can restore the physical frame of the  appellant.

That is why it has been said by Courts that whenever any Mohd. Mursid @ Bablu vs Rajesh Ohri on 25 February, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/44431814/
6  amount is determined as the compensation payable for any injury suffered  during an accident, the object is to compensate such injured "so far as  money can compensate" because it is impossible to equate the money with  the human sufferings or personal deprivations.

sentences.text: Money cannot renew a  broken and shattered physical frame.

.............................................................
............................................................. In its very nature whenever a Tribunal, or a Court is required to fix the amount of compensation in cases of accident, it involves some guess work, some hypothetical consideration, some amount of sympathy linked with the nature of the disability caused.
But all the aforesaid elements have to be viewed with objective standards.

................................When compensation is to be awarded for pain and suffering and loss of amenity of life, the special circumstances of the claimant have to be taken into account including his age, the unusual deprivation he has suffered, the effect thereof on his future life."
36. In JAGDISH VS. MOHAN (Supra), it was further observed as under: "11.
In making the computation in the present case, the court must be mindful of the fact that the appellant has suffered a serious disability in which he has suffered loss of use of both his hands.
For a person engaged in manual activities, it requires no stretch of imagination to understand that loss of hands is a complete deprivation of the ability to earn.
Nothing, at least in the facts of this case, can restore lost hands.
But the measure of compensation must reflect a genuine attempt of the law to restore the dignity of the being.
Our yardsticks of compensation should not be so abysmal as to lead one to question whether our law values human life.
If it does, as it must, it must provide a realistic recompense for the pain of loss and trauma of suffering.
Awards of compensation are not law's doles.
In a discourse of rights, they constitute entitlements under law.
Our conversations about law must shift from a paternalistic subordination of the individual to an assertion of enforceable rights as intrinsic to human dignity.
The Tribunal has noted that appellant is unable to even eat or to attend to a visit to the toilet without the assistance of an attendant.
In this background, it would be a denial of justice to compute the disability at 90 per cent.
The disability is indeed total.
Having regard to the age of the appellant, the Tribunal applied multiplier of 18.
In the circumstances, the compensation payable to the appellant on account of the loss of income, including future prospects, would be Rs.18,14,400.

In addition to this amount, the appellant should be granted an amount of Rs.2,00,000/ on account of pain,
suffering and loss of amenities.
The amount awarded by the Tribunal towards medical expenses (Rs.98,908); for extra nourishment (Rs.25,000) and for attendant's expenses (Rs.1,00,000) is maintained.
The Tribunal has declined to award any amount towards future treatment.
The appellant should be allowed an amount of Rs.3,00,000 for future medical expenses.
The appellant is thus awarded a total sum of Rs.25,38,308 by way of compensation.
The appellant would be entitled to interest at the rate of 9 per cent per annum on the compensation from the date of filing of the claim petition.
The liability to pay compensation has been fastened by the Tribunal and by the High Court on the insurer, owner and driver jointly and severally which is affirmed.

LIABILITY 41.

Admittedly, the offending vehicle was insured with respondent No.3/Insurance Company as on the date of accident i.e. 14.11.2013, however, the claim was resisted on the ground that petitioner was not holding any driving licence as on the date of the accident.

Learned counsel for insurance company also relied upon the judgment of Rehmani Begum Vs. Krishan Pal decided on 18.01.2019 by Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in MAC Appeal No.954/2017.
42.
It is relevant to mention here that no evidence was adduced by the insurance company to prove that petitioner did not hold a valid driving licence as on the date of the accident.

Also, presuming that the petitioner did not have a valid driving licence, it is settled law that if the accident had taken place due to negligence of the driver of the offending vehicle, then in that scenario even if the petitioner did not hold a valid driving licence, the same was immaterial.
Also, the ratio of Rehmani Begum (supra) is not attracted to the facts and circumstances to the present case.

In the instant case, it is already held that it was respondent No.1/drivercumowner of the offending vehicle, who was negligent and had caused the accident.
43. In view of aforesaid circumstances, it is accordingly held that insurance company is under the statutory liability to pay the compensation to the petitioner.

However, since it is proved that respondent No.1/Rajesh Ohri was the driver cumowner of the offending vehicle at the time of accident, hence, he is liable to pay compensation as the accident took place due to his rash and negligent driving.
Therefore, both the respondents are jointly and severally liable to pay compensation to the petitioner.
RELIEF 44.
In view of above findings on Issue Nos.1 & 2, I award an amount of Rs.34,46,000/ (Rupees Thirty Four Lakh Forty Six thousand) as compensation to petitioner Mohd.Mursid.
Petitioner is also entitled to interest @ 9% per annum from the date of filing of the DAR i.e. 15.12.2014 till its realisation.
Amount of Interim Award, if paid any, be deducted from the compensation amount.
45. Consequently, interest amount be paid to the petitioner along with award amount as per the terms and conditions mentioned in succeeding paragraphs.

The said fact  is also corroborated by the site plan and Mechanical Inspection Reports of both  the vehicles which reflect that the offending vehicle was damaged from the left  lower side whereas, the scooty being driven by the petitioner was damaged from  the front lower portion.

Accordingly, issue  No.1 is decided in favour of the petitioner and against the respondents.
The provision of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 ("the Act", for short) makes   clear that the award must be just, which means that compensation should, to  the extent possible, fully and adequately restore the claimant to the position  prior to the accident.
The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss  suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair,
 reasonable and equitable manner.
The court or the Tribunal shall have to  assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation  or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability an  its consequences, is inevitable
. A person is not only to be compensated for th  physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such  injury.
